abstract: Wind-power events connect atmospheric variability to operational decisions, but their usefulness depends on which distinctions survive measurement and compression. We introduce a four-layer framework linking detection, matching, representation and evaluation through structural survival, independent physical tracking and forecast-to-cost tests. Seventeen detector configurations span seven primary archives with 333 turbines, supplemented by a seven-turbine instrumented French site and three observers' assessments of 320 real windows. Ordered trajectories provide a transferable structural reference. For signed-domain angular images, a trajectory and its sign reversal coincide; protecting one polarity coordinate restores a physically relevant distinction. Chronological calibration against independent light detection and ranging observations raises directional area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.494/0.477 to 0.890/0.905 at two instruments. In a separate native-resolution forecast experiment, a pipeline combining historical shape and issued weather forecasts reduces simulated four-hour accuracy charges under a documented Jiangsu rule by 18.2% relative to persistence. A same-model action comparison further shows how lower charges can accompany higher average error. Together, these results establish a task-aware route from transferable event structure to physical information and rule-based economic evaluation.
highlights: Protocol-aware measurement separates event stability from physical information.
Protecting polarity restores wind-tendency discrimination after angular encoding.
Independent LiDAR tests connect event representations to measured wind changes.
Issued shape-and-weather forecasts reduce rule-based four-hour charges by 18.2%.
Three observers anchor event-presence evaluation across 320 real windows.
